newsitem.title: USA: Red River to stay high after tributary breaks dike.
newsitem.headline: Red River to stay high after tributary breaks dike.

text.p: Residents were on high alert along the Red River on Monday as burst dikes and ice blockages increased the strain on makeshift barriers built to hold back flood waters.

Earthen and sandbag dikes built as temporary barriers to hold back the water will be tested longer than expected, said Dennis Walaker, director of operations at the Public Works Department in Fargo, North Dakota's biggest city.
The Red River was at 37.65 feet Monday in Fargo, more than 20 feet over flood stage, and should remain at that level through the week, he said.

The Sheyenne River, which feeds into the Red River north of Fargo, burst through dikes south of the city this weekend merging with the Wild Rice River, which flows into the Red River south of Fargo. The Red River flows north into Canada.
"Right now we don't really anticipate any significant drop in the river for three or four days," Walaker said.
"I don't know if we will see any higher water. But, we have added to the time we will be at the highest levels," he said.
Residents evacuated some towns north of Fargo.
Emergency crews said ice on the Red River slowed its flow north and backed water into tributaries creating additional flooding along these waterways.

In Perley and Hendrum, Minnesota, about 15 miles north of Fargo, most residents evacuated. Dikes around these towns of about 150 people have held, said John Korzeniowski, spokesman for the Norman County, Minnesota, Flood Management Team.
In Grand Forks, 90 miles north of Fargo, residents prepared for the Red River to crest later this week at 49 feet, or 21 feet above flood stage. On Monday the river was just under 44 feet.
"We've filled about 1.3 million sandbags and have about another 700,000 to go," said Rick Coulter, acting Emergency Management Officer in Grand Forks, a city of 71,000.

Two of three bridges connecting Grand Forks to East Grand Forks, Minnesota, should close this week, said Coulter. The Point Bridge, in downtown Grand Forks, would close when the river reaches 44.3 feet, and the Sorlie Bridge, also downtown, would close at 46.75 feet.
